title: Mumbai's Dedicated Pasta Restaurants Boom as World Pasta Day Arrives October 25
excerpt: Pasta bars built around hand-rolled shapes are drawing queues and expanding across Bandra, Lower Parel and Versova, as Mumbai marks World Pasta Day on October 25 with 28 listed dishes and a hands-on pasta-making workshop.
body:
• Mumbai marks World Pasta Day on Sunday, October 25 with a dining scene in which pasta is no longer a side dish on Italian menus — dedicated pasta bars and pasta-first restaurants are drawing queues and expanding.
  • Bandra's Pomodoro, a pasta and coffee bar founded by sisters Afshaa and Nousheen Rajqotwala, grew from 28 seats to more than 60 in under a year on the strength of handmade pasta and a live pasta bar.
  • Femina's World Pasta Day roundup lists 28 pasta dishes across Mumbai, from a Rs 475 creamy mushroom fettuccine in Versova to a Rs 1,350 lemon-ricotta agnolotti in Bandra.
  • Luuma House in Juhu is running a hands-on pasta-making workshop on October 25 from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m., where guests roll, shape and cook their own pasta.

Pasta has moved to the centre of the plate in Mumbai. Ahead of World Pasta Day on October 25, The Hindu reports that dedicated pasta restaurants are booming in the city — a shift visible in the queues outside Bandra pasta bars, in menus built entirely around hand-rolled shapes, and in the number of kitchens now treating pasta as the main event rather than one course among many.

A pasta bar that had to double in size

The clearest sign of the trend is Pomodoro, the neighbourhood Italian pasta and coffee bar on 16th Road in Bandra West. Founded by sisters Chef Afshaa Rajqotwala and Nousheen Rajqotwala, it began as a 28-seater and expanded into a 60-plus-seat outlet in less than a year, according to Restaurant India. The expansion, the report said, came in response to steady demand from repeat diners, and the restaurant kept its live pasta bar at the centre of the room, with fresh pasta made by hand and sauces prepared from scratch.

"Pomodoro was never meant to be about scale. It was built around care, for the food, for the people we serve, and for the neighbourhood that welcomed us so openly. This expansion isn't a business milestone as much as it is a thank you. Same food, same values, just a little more space to share it."

— Chef Afshaa Rajqotwala, via Restaurant India

Esquire India described the long queue outside Pomodoro and its Le Cordon Bleu-trained chef's hand-rolled pastas, naming the Herbed Burrata Ravioli, Chicken Parm and Seafood Vongole as must-tries.

What World Pasta Day looks like on the ground

The depth of the scene shows in the range of dishes restaurants are putting forward for October 25. Femina's World Pasta Day list runs to 28 dishes: Pomodoro's Lasagna Verde, built on herbed pasta sheets, seasonal vegetables and a tomato-and-cheese fonduta at Rs 755; Tablespoon's freshly made Vodka Rigatoni at Lower Parel at Rs 985; Adelina's handcrafted agnolotti filled with lemon-infused ricotta at Rs 1,350; and CinCin's Piedmont-style agnolotti at Rs 945 onwards. At the more accessible end, Tora in Versova serves a Creamy Mushroom Fettuccine at Rs 475 and BaaMee in Andheri a Three Cheese Ravioli at Rs 595, while Trapdoor in Versova goes furthest from the classics with squid ink pasta and baby octopus at Rs 899.

Mumbai's versions also bend toward local tastes. Femina's list includes a butter chicken mac and cheese at 1BHK in Jogeshwari West, at Rs 795, alongside traditional plates such as Toscano's spaghetti aglio olio e peperoncino.

Beyond the restaurant table

The boom is not only about eating out. Hospitality News notes that Luuma House in Juhu is marking World Pasta Day with a hands-on workshop on Sunday, October 25, from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m., where guests roll, shape and prepare pasta from scratch before cooking and eating what they made. Its regular menu carries a porcini veil spinach ravioli at Rs 655. Workshops of that kind point to where the trend is heading: pasta as a craft home cooks want to learn, not just a dish they order.

What it means for diners

For readers visiting Mumbai — or returning home for the festive season — the practical takeaway is that the city's best pasta is now concentrated in dedicated rooms in Bandra West, Khar, Lower Parel and Versova, and the popular ones fill up: Esquire notes the queue outside Pomodoro as a fixture, so booking ahead or arriving early is the sensible move this weekend. Prices for a headline pasta dish run from about Rs 475 to Rs 1,350 before taxes, a spread that puts the trend within reach of a casual lunch as well as a celebration dinner.

The next test is staying power. Pomodoro's answer — expand the room, keep the live pasta bar, change nothing about the food — suggests restaurateurs believe the demand is structural, driven by diners who can tell hand-rolled from factory-made.
